To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fetal lung fibroblast-conditioned medium contains insulin-like activity and that this insulin-like activity is IGF-I.
the insulin-like growth factors I and II (IGF-I and IGF-II) are synthesized in human lung tissue and that their synthesis is regulated by growth hormone (GH).
fetal lung fibro­ blasts secrete and respond (via the IGF-I receptors) to IGF-I.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of IGF-I in the regulation of fetal growth.
growth factors that act in a paracrine or autocrine mode in fetal life and with the regulation of their expression.
the regulation of growth in fetal life.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence that the IGFs are the only factors involved in the regulation of fetal lung growth.

IGFs and IGF binding proteins are present in many fetal tissues, that they are synthesized by many cell types in response to local requirements, that they act locally, and that they are important regulators of fetal growth and development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fetal lung is a major source of IGFs in utero.
IGF-I is the principal somatomedin in fetal life and that IGF-I and IGF-II are both important for fetal growth and develop­ ment.
the fetal rat lung contains a large amount of IGF-I mRNA, which is regulated by the fetal pituitary, and that IGF-I is secreted in a manner that is regulated by the pituitary and by the lung itself.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a lot to learn about how these growth factors work together to regulate growth in the lung.
IGF-I plays a role in lung growth and that this role is mediated in part through the EGF receptor.
the IGF-I system is an important component in the regulation of lung development and that it may be possible to use the IGF-I gene to stimulate lung growth and repair.
